evidence.claim: IEA Energy and AI states that global data-center investment nearly doubled since 2022 and reached about half a trillion dollars in 2024; it also notes that new transmission lines can take four to eight years in advanced economies and that wait times for critical components such as transformers and cables have doubled in the past three years.
evidence.source_title: IEA Energy and AI - Executive Summary

evidence.claim: DOE's supply-chain materials state that distribution-transformer lead times increased from three to six months in 2019 to 12 to 30 months in 2023, driven by supply, labor, and material constraints.
evidence.source_title: DOE Supply Chain and Market Analysis

evidence.claim: Comfort Systems USA's FY2025 Form 10-K describes the company as a provider of mechanical and electrical contracting services, including HVAC, plumbing, piping, controls, off-site construction, monitoring, fire protection, and electrical installation/service across commercial, industrial, and institutional markets.

Comfort Systems USA's FY2025 Form 10-K reported that demand increased especially strongly in the technology sector, electrical-segment revenue rose 61.9% to $2.43 billion, and backlog at December 31, 2025 was $11.94 billion, up 99.3% from December 31, 2024.

Stem's FY2025 Form 10-K describes managed services for design, procurement, commissioning, operation, and optimization of energy storage and hybrid systems enabled by PowerTrack Optimizer software; the filing also states that the financial statements assume going-concern status and reports cash of $48.9 million, accumulated deficit of $1.49 billion, and negative working capital at December 31, 2025.

Enphase's FY2025 Form 10-K filing is available as a Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, filed February 17, 2026; the filing frames Enphase around distributed energy systems and grid participation.

SolarEdge's FY2025 Form 10-K describes the company as a global smart energy technology company and notes the launch of the next-generation SolarEdge Nexis residential product portfolio with initial units delivered near the end of 2025.

Generac's 2025 sustainability materials discuss megatrends of lower power quality and higher power demand and refer to rising demand for backup power across data centers, telecom, and critical applications; they also cite ecobee Grid Resiliency enrollment scale.

AZZ's FY2025 annual report describes the company as a provider of hot-dip galvanizing and metal-coatings services for critical infrastructure; this supports a second-order infrastructure durability mapping but not yet a quantified utility/transmission revenue mix.

EnerSys FY2025 sustainability materials describe the company as powering mission-critical systems across defense, secure communications, and other essential systems, supporting the critical-power mapping but requiring segment-materiality verification.

CBAK Energy's FY2025 Form 10-K reports annual capacity of 1.0 GWh for legacy model 26650 cells at the Dalian manufacturing center and states that gross profit margin declined to 9.4% in 2025 from 24% in 2024, aligned with a drop in sales of batteries for residential energy supply and UPS applications.

Tetra Tech's investor site lists a 2025 annual report; external search context identifies Tetra Tech as maintaining a strong position in environmental, water, consulting, and engineering markets, which supports a permitting/water/engineering mapping but not a pure grid-hardware mapping.

AECOM's FY2025 annual report describes planning, consulting, advisory, architectural and engineering design, construction management, and program management services across transportation, facilities, environmental, energy, water, and government end markets; AECOM reported $23.4 billion of design backlog for FY2025.

Jacobs FY2025 annual-report materials refer to prior Critical Mission Solutions work spanning areas including clean energy transition and nuclear decommissioning and cleanup, supporting a broad technical-services mapping rather than a pure-play power-chain mapping.

APi Group FY2025 annual-report search context identifies transmission and distribution services as installation and maintenance services for electrical transmission and distribution, with demand drivers including grid modernization, renewable-power buildout, rate-case dynamics, and infrastructure spending.
evidence.source_title: APi Group FY2025 Annual Report and 10-K

memory_update.text: FIX should be promoted within this candidate chunk as the clearest visible execution-bottleneck mapping: data-center/technology-sector mechanical and electrical contracting demand, FY2025 technology-sector strength, electrical-segment growth, and backlog growth are directly disclosed.

ENS remains an underfollowed critical-power candidate: industrial battery label may obscure mission-critical backup exposure, but data-center/telecom/utility segment materiality must be proven before ranking it above core grid hardware names.

AZZ is a second-order grid-buildout candidate through galvanizing/metal coatings for critical infrastructure; the key survival test is whether utility/transmission/electrical infrastructure is a material volume and pricing driver.

GNRC has plausible backup-power and distributed-resilience exposure, including telecom and potential data-center demand, but residential generator cyclicality and outage-driven demand make it less pure than grid hardware or data-center electrical contractors.

ENPH and SEDG are real distributed-energy power-electronics companies, but their relationship to the Energy and Power Chain is grid-edge flexibility rather than AI data-center critical-path power infrastructure; both require market-pricing and residential-solar-cycle checks.

TTEK, ACM, J, and APG are services/execution reference or underfollowed candidates. They may benefit from permitting, engineering, water, fire/safety, and infrastructure maintenance bottlenecks, but each needs end-market/backlog materiality verification.

STEM, SEDG, and CBAT should remain speculative_shadow until financial-quality gates are passed. STEM has going-concern and working-capital concerns; CBAT has low gross margin and customer/product-validation risk; SEDG needs proof of durable recovery from prior solar-channel stress.
Need current market-cap, valuation, analyst-coverage, short-interest, and earnings-revision checks for every ticker before classifying them as truly underfollowed or already consensus.
Need latest 2026 quarterly reports and transcripts for FIX, ENS, GNRC, AZZ, ENPH, SEDG, STEM, CBAT, TTEK, ACM, J, and APG to confirm whether FY2025 evidence continued into 2026.
Candidate chunk visible to the model was truncated after APi Group; later Layer 2B calls should verify whether additional tickers were omitted from this chunk before final scoring.

summary: Mapped the visible candidate chunk into Serenity Layer 2B ticker relationships. This chunk is not the core transformer/switchgear chokepoint; it is mainly a grid-edge, backup power, storage, engineering/permitting, mechanical/electrical execution, and second-order infrastructure-services basket. The highest-quality relationship in this chunk is FIX as a data-center mechanical/electrical execution beneficiary, supported by 2025 backlog and technology-sector disclosures. ENS, GNRC, ENPH, AZZ, TTEK, ACM, J, and APG remain plausible but require segment-materiality checks. STEM, SEDG, and CBAT are speculative shadow names where financial quality and end-market proof are gating issues.
